title: Characterizing interaction between the juxtamembrane region of the single transmembrane protein and membrane using chemically synthesized peptides
protocol: Weigh 400 mg of NovaPEG Rink Amide resin (0.25 mmol/g).
Vortex the resin in dimethylformamide (DMF, 2 mL) for 10 min at 25°C.
Let the resin precipitate by gravity and remove the solvent.
Place the resin on the Liberty Blue peptide synthesizer.
Type in the peptide sequence on the synthesizer.
Set the scale for the synthesis to 0.1 mmol.
Deprotect Fmoc groups at 75°C for 15 s and then at 90°C for 50 s using 10% piperazine with 0.1 M HOBt in NMP.
Couple all residues except His, Cys, and Arg by heating to 75°C for 15 s and then to 90°C for 110 s with DIC and HOBt (0.5 mmol each).
For His residues, couple at 25°C for 120 s and then at 50°C for 480 s using DIC and HOBt (0.5 mmol each).
For Cys residues, perform the single coupling reaction under the same conditions as His.
For Arg residues, use OxymaPure instead of HOBt in addition to DIC and couple twice: first at 75°C for 15 s and then at 90°C for 180 s.
Run peptide synthesis on the synthesizer with an average cycle time of 5 min except for His and Cys residues, which take about 10 min each, and Arg residues, which take about 12 min each.
Collect the peptide resin in a glass vial after post-treatment.
Pour methanol into the vial to wash the peptide resin and then remove methanol by decantation.
Repeat washing cycle three times.
Dry the resin under vacuum overnight.
Mix water (50 μL), triisopropylsilane (TIS, 50 μL), 3,6-Dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol (50 μL), and Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA, 1850 μL) in a glass tube.
Weigh 100 mg of the peptide resin in a Falcon tube.
Add the cleavage cocktail to the resin in the Falcon tube.
Shake the mixture on a high-speed mixer for 2.5 hours at 25°C.
Optionally, stir the mixture using a stirring bar magnet with a magnetic stirrer.
Prepare an ISOLUTE double fritted filtration column and place it on a cramp.
Place a 15 mL Falcon tube under the filtration column.
Pour the reaction mixture through the filter to separate it from the resin component.
Pass the solution into the Falcon tube.
Connect one end of a gas hose to an Ar gas cylinder.
Attach a 200 μL pipet tip to the other end of the gas hose and insert it into the Falcon tube.
Direct a slow stream of Ar gas to remove the solvent component of the reaction mixture.
Add cold diethyl ether up to the top of the Falcon tube to precipitate the peptide component.
Spin down the white solid and decant out the supernatant, diethyl ether.
Repeat the process of adding diethyl ether, vortexing, spinning down, and decanting the supernatant for three times.
Add a mixture of acetonitrile and water (1/1 ratio, total 8 mL) to the resultant solid.
Lyophilize overnight at 25°C.
Set up conditions for RP-HPLC purification.
Check solubility of crude powder in a mixture of acetonitrile and water.
Take a small amount (less than 0.1 mg) of the crude powder into a microtube.
Add 100 μL of ddH2O to the microtube.
Add 10 μL of acetonitrile to the microtube.
Prepare ddH2O containing TFA (0.1% v/v) and acetonitrile (HPLC grade) containing TFA (0.1% v/v).
Attach the ODS column (10 mm × 250 mm) in the system.
Set a gradient program on the HPLC machine with an initial concentration of acetonitrile solution at 30%, increasing to 60% over 30 minutes.
Set the flow rate to 2.5 mL/min.
Set the detecting wavelength to 220 nm.
Run the program several times without injecting the sample.
Optional: Change the acetonitrile solution to a mixture of 2-propanol and acetonitrile (1/1) containing 0.1% TFA (v/v).
Optional: Use a C4 column instead.
Take 0.1 mg of the crude powder and dissolve it in an eluent mixture with initial acetonitrile concentration.
Dissolution volume can vary between 100 μL to 500 μL, as long as the entire crude powder dissolves.
Prepare microtubes (1.5 mL) for manually collecting peaks from the HPLC elution profile.
Collect ∼10 drops (∼50 μL) of eluent at the peak top for mass analysis.
Collect a fraction with peptide components condensed for MALDI-TOF-MS analysis.
Change the gradient program if peaks on the elution profile overlap or no apparent peak is collectible.
Increase the length of time for the gradient from 25 min to 40 min or so to separate peaks.
Dump the microtube with collected sample into liquid nitrogen to freeze it.
Subject the frozen sample to lyophilization.
Place matrix powder (0.5 mg) in a microtube (0.5 mL).
Add a mixture of acetonitrile and water (1:1, 200 μL) to the matrix powder.
Lyophilize the sample from step d.
Add 10 μL of the supernatant from the matrix prepared previously to the lyophilized powder.
Mix the solution with the powder thoroughly.
Place 2 μL of the sample solution on a sample plate for mass measurement.
Perform mass analysis.
Repeat steps f through h for all fractionated samples.
Take 0.1 mg of crude powder in a microtube (1.5 mL).
Dissolve it into the eluent mixture with the initial acetonitrile concentration, varying volume from 100 μL to 500 μL.
Inject the solution for purification.
Weigh 1 mg of peptide resin in a microtube.
Dissolve Alexa Fluor 568 C5 Maleimide (0.28 mg) in DMF (100 μL).
Add the dissolved Alexa Fluor solution to the microtube containing peptide resin.
Add diisopropylethylamine (DIEA, 2 μL) to start the reaction at 25°C.
Cover the reaction mixture with aluminum foil.
Prepare RP-HPLC conditions as previously described.
Change the detecting wavelength to 575 nm for fluorescent dye detection.
After 2 hours from derivatization start, take 2 μL of reaction solution.
Inject the taken solution into RP-HLC for analysis.
Run RP-HLC and collect the peak at a similar elution time to the unlabeled peptide.
Collect the eluent at the peak top.
Measure the mass of the component in the fraction.
After 24 hours from derivatization start, begin purification with RP-HLC.
Inject samples into RP-HLC for purification.
Cover samples with aluminum foil to prevent photobleaching.
Freeze the eluted solution directly for lyophilization.
Weigh peptide (1.5 × 10−7 mol, 1 mg), POPC (1.2 × 10−5 mol, 8.8 mg), POPS (0.3 × 10−5 mol, 3.0 mg), and octyl-β-D-glucoside (50 mg) in a glass vial.
Mix the components with chloroform and methanol (10:3).
Remove organic solvents under a stream of argon gas.
Dry the mixture under vacuum for 18 hours.
Add MOPS buffer (pH: 7.0; 1 mL) to the solid residue.
Stir using a magnetic stirrer at 37°C for 4 hours.
Put the solution into a dialysis bag (cutoff: 3000 Da) and start dialysis.
Change the dialysis buffer after 1 h on day 1.
Change the dialysis buffer again after 3 h on day 1.
Change the dialysis buffer two times on day 2.
Prepare the sample solution for analysis of polarized FT-IR on day 3.
Take out the solution from the dialysis bag and put it into a vial or microtube.
Keep the sample at 4°C.
Weigh peptide (1.5 × 10−9 mol, 10 μg), POPC (1.2 × 10−7 mol, 88 μg), POPS (3 × 10−7 mol, 30 μg), and octyl-β-D-glucoside (37.5 mg) in a microtube.
Mix the weighed components with a mixture of chloroform and methanol (10:3) in a volume of 3 mL.
Remove organic solvents under a stream of Ar gas.
Dry the sample under reduced pressure for 18 hours.
Cover the sample with aluminum foil to protect from light.
Add MOPS buffer (pH 7.0; 750 μL) to the solid and stir using a magnetic stirrer at 37°C for 4 hours.
Place the solution into a dialysis bag and start dialysis.
Change the dialysis buffer after 1 hour on day 1.
Change the dialysis buffer again after 3 hours on day 1.
Change the dialysis buffer two times on day 2.
Remove the solution from the dialysis bag on day 3.
Transfer the solution into a microtube (1.5 mL in size).
Keep the sample at 4°C for no more than 48 hours before fluorescence measurement.
Prepare an extruder system with a polycarbonate filter of 100 nm pore size.
Extrude the sample solution 21 times and the sample is ready for fluorescence measurement.
Perform polarized attenuated total reflection (ATR) FT-IR experiment for evaluation of reconstitution and structural analysis.
Place a germanium internal reflection element without any sample.
Set the polarizer to 90 degrees to produce parallel polarized light.
Close the sample room and fill it with nitrogen gas.
Scan the instrument 1,000 times to obtain the background spectrum for the parallel polarized light.
Set the polarizer to 0 degrees to produce perpendicular polarized light.
Repeat steps involving setting up the instrument with the new polarizer orientation to obtain a background spectrum for perpendicular polarized light.
Take the sample solution (50 μL) and spread it on the germanium plate.
Direct a slow flow of nitrogen gas at an oblique angle to the IR plate to blow up water components, forming an oriented multilamellar peptide-lipid film.
Repeat spreading another 50 μL of the sample solution over the existing film.
Repeat the procedure one additional time to form layered films.
Place the germanium plate with the peptide-lipid film having been layered.
Set the polarizer to 90 degrees to produce parallel polarized light.
Close the sample room and fill it with nitrogen gas.
Scan it 1000 times, which gives the resulting spectrum for the parallel polarized light.
Set the polarizer to 0 degrees to produce perpendicular polarized light.
Close the sample room and fill it with nitrogen gas.
Scan it 1000 times, which gives the resulting spectrum for the perpendicular polarized light.
Subtract the background from the resulting spectrum for each obtained in e. and f. to get final results.
Export these spectra as a comma-separated value file (.csv) for the next analysis step.
Load the spectrum in csv format into Fityk.
Focus on the spectral region from 1600 to 1700 cm−1 for amide I frequency analysis.
Identify peaks corresponding to α-helix (1648‒1660 cm−1), aggregated strand (1610‒1628 cm−1, 1675‒1695 cm−1), and β-sheet (1625‒1640 cm−1, 1675‒1695 cm−1).
Introduce Gaussian peaks for curve fitting.
Adjust the peak parameters to fit the experimental spectrum accurately.
Press the “auto-peak” button until a peak appears at the maximum or shoulder on the spectrum.
Press the “Start-fitting” button to fit the curve.
Export the result for output.
Calculate the area of the introduced peak.
Click on the peak representing α-helix and read its value in the window.
Repeat all procedures for spectra from parallel polarized light.
Repeat all procedures for spectra from perpendicular polarized light.
Calculate the dichroic ratio using the observed dichroic ratio (RATR).
Use the equation S m e a s = \frac{E_x^2 - RATR E_y^2 + E_z^2}{E_x^2 - RATR E_y^2 - 2 E_z^2} to calculate the order parameter.
Substitute the electric field amplitudes: \( E_x = 1.399 \), \( E_y = 1.514 \), and \( E_z = 1.621 \).
Calculate the angle between the helix director and the membrane normal.
Use a value of 41.8° for the angle between the helix director and the transition-dipole moment of the amide I vibration mode.
Apply a Smem value of 0.85 in the calculation.
Weigh 58 μg of PI(4,5)P2 on a microbalance.
Add a mixture of chloroform and methanol (1:1, 2 mL) to the PI(4,5)P2.
Divide the PI(4,5)P2 solution into 20 microtubes (1.5 mL each).
Remove the organic solvent from all microtubes and store them at -20°C.
Turn on the fluorescence spectrometer and temperature regulation unit.
Set the temperature to 37°C.
Set the excitation wavelength to 568 nm and scanning wavelength from 580 to 660 nm.
Pipette 500 μL of sample solution into a quartz cuvette with a path length of 1 cm.
Wait for 20 minutes after placing the cuvette in the spectrometer.
Scan the sample.
Transfer the sample solution back to its original microtube.
Take all 750 μL of the sample solution and mix it with PI(4,5)P2 prepared previously.
Vortex the mixture for 2 minutes to allow diffusion without sonication.
Pipette out 500 μL of the new sample solution and place it in a cuvette.
Wait for 20 minutes after placing the cuvette in the spectrometer.
Scan the sample again.
Repeat steps from mixing with PI(4,5)P2 through scanning to increase the concentration of PI(4,5)P2 as needed.
Export results for analysis.
Perform molecular dynamics simulation to gain insight into the interaction between the juxtamembrane region and the membrane.
Prepare files for molecular dynamics (MD) simulation.
Build a starting structure for Mps3 using Pymol’s "Build" module.
Set the putative transmembrane region as an α-helical structure in Pymol.
Assign an extended structure configuration to the juxtamembrane region in Pymol.
Save the built structure as a pdb file.
Load the starting structure on the Charmm-gui website for MD simulation preparation.
Choose “Input Generator”, then select “Membrane Builder” and proceed to “Bilayer builder”.
Check “Align the First Principal Axis Along Z” for determining orientation of transmembrane helix relative to membrane in web page "Orientation options".
Click on “Next Step” to view peptide orientation in the membrane.
If the orientation shown is not desirable, go back to previous page and adjust “Positioning Options”.
Ensure center of the transmembrane region closely matches the center of the membrane.
Ensure transmembrane region is perpendicular to the membrane.
Check “Translate Molecule along Z axis” and enter a value in Angstrom for vertical movement to place transmembrane region at the center of the membrane.
Extract the downloaded file from the Charmm-gui website in your working directory.
Open the extracted folder and navigate to the "namd" directory.
Run "./namd2 +idlepoll +p32 +devices 0,1 step6.1_equilibration.inp > WT6.1.log".
Run "./namd2 +idlepoll +p32 +devices 0,1 step6.2_equilibration.inp > WT6.2.log".
Run "./namd2 +idlepoll +p32 +devices 0,1 step6.3_equilibration.inp > WT6.3.log".
Run "./namd2 +idlepoll +p32 +devices 0,1 step6.4_equilibration.inp > WT6.4.log".
Run "./namd2 +idlepoll +p32 +devices 0,1 step6.5_equilibration.inp > WT6.5.log".
Run the NAMD simulation using the command: ./namd2 +idlepoll +p32 +devices 0,1 step7.1_production.inp > WT7.1.log
Visualize the trajectory of the simulation using software such as VMD.
